claims.text: Introducing graphene nanoplatelets into a high-entropy alloy will reduce its coefficient of friction.
Introducing graphene nanoplatelets into a high-entropy alloy will reduce its wear rate.
The friction and wear benefits will persist from approximately -50°C to 600°C.
The graphene-containing composite will remain effective under moderate-to-high sliding contact.
Graphene nanoplatelets will segregate at grain boundaries or form an interconnected network in the alloy.
The graphene distribution will promote formation of a stable transfer film during sliding.
The graphene-derived transfer film will continuously renew lubrication at the contact interface.
Graphene's layered structure provides low shear strength under mechanical stress.
A graphene-derived self-lubricating film will reduce direct asperity contact.
Reduced direct asperity contact will lower friction and wear.
The graphene-doped alloy will have a coefficient of friction at least 20-30% lower than the untreated alloy.
The graphene-doped alloy will have an approximately order-of-magnitude lower wear rate than the untreated alloy.
Uneven graphene distribution may limit the tribological benefit.
Graphene content below that required to form an effective lubricating network may limit the benefit.
Temperatures or loads exceeding the transfer film's stability range may eliminate the benefit.
Prior literature in related material systems supports adding self-lubricating carbon-based phases to improve tribological performance.

contradictions.description: Uneven distribution or graphene degradation is presented as a boundary condition under which efficacy is not expected, but the falsification rule also treats poor distribution or degradation as falsifying the underlying hypothesis. A failed implementation therefore could be labeled both an excluded condition and a decisive refutation.
